slides.title: Kaplan-Meier Survival Estimator & The Onboarding Valley of Death

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova (Senior Architect)
solo.title: Kaplan-Meier Survival Estimator & The Onboarding Valley of Death

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: The Kaplan-Meier product-limit estimator computes the non-parametric cumulative probability of surviving past time t, adjusting for censored accounts at risk in each step.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Plotting S-hat of t reveals the famous Onboarding Valley of Death: over 31 percent of customer churn occurs during the first 3 months of contract inception. Beyond month 12, the hazard rate flattens into an exponential survival plateau.

solo.contentHtml:
The Kaplan-Meier Product-Limit Estimator & Hazard Curves

Non-parametric survival estimation in the presence of right-censoring.

Kaplan-Meier Product-Limit Formula (1958)
$$\hat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_i \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_i}{n_i}\right)$$
  • • $t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_m$: ordered distinct event times.
  • • $d_i$: number of churn terminations at time $t_i$.
  • • $n_i$: number of active accounts at risk immediately prior to $t_i$.
The Onboarding "Valley of Death"

Analyzing $\hat{S}(t)$ across contract cohorts unveils dramatic hazard shifts:

• Month 1 to 3 Hazard Spike: Over $31\%$ of all churn terminations occur in the first 90 days (onboarding friction / billing surprises).
• Post-Month 12 Plateau: Hazard rate $\lambda(t) = \frac{d_i}{n_i \Delta t}$ drops by $82\%$, stabilizing into a loyal baseline.

duo.title: Kaplan-Meier Survival Estimator & The Onboarding Valley of Death

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Look at the survival step function! The steepest drop is right at months one, two, and three! If a customer survives past month twelve, their probability of staying loyal for years shoots through the roof!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Precisely. That initial drop is the onboarding 'Valley of Death'. Without Kaplan-Meier analysis, an executive might pour marketing dollars into twenty-month-old accounts when the real retention crisis is happening during the first thirty days.

slides.title: Greenwood's Variance Formula & Confidence Envelopes

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova (Senior Architect)
solo.title: Greenwood's Variance Formula & Confidence Envelopes

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: To establish rigorous statistical bounds on survival curves, Major Greenwood derived the asymptotic variance of S-hat of t in 1926 via the delta method applied to log survival.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Notice how Greenwood's formula scales by S-hat squared times the summation of d-sub-i divided by n-sub-i times n-sub-i minus d-sub-i. As sample cohorts diminish in the late tenure tail, risk denominators shrink, widening the confidence envelope.

solo.contentHtml:
Greenwood's Asymptotic Variance Formula (1926)

Delta method derivation for non-parametric survival confidence intervals.

Greenwood's Variance Expression
$$\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat{S}(t)) = [\hat{S}(t)]^2 \sum_{t_i \le t} \frac{d_i}{n_i (n_i - d_i)}$$

Asymptotic 95% Confidence Band:

$$\text{CI}_{0.95}(t) = \left[ \hat{S}(t) \pm 1.96 \sqrt{\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat{S}(t))} \right]$$
Delta Method Derivation Sketch

Apply log transformation $\ln \hat{S}(t) = \sum_{t_i \le t} \ln(1 - d_i/n_i)$:

Conditional binomial variance: $\text{Var}(d_i \mid n_i) = n_i p_i (1-p_i) = n_i \frac{d_i}{n_i} (1 - \frac{d_i}{n_i})$
By first-order Taylor expansion on $\ln(1 - x)$:
$$\text{Var}(\ln \hat{S}(t)) \approx \sum_{t_i \le t} \frac{d_i}{n_i (n_i - d_i)}$$
By delta method on $g(u) = e^u$: $\text{Var}(e^u) = (e^u)^2 \text{Var}(u) \quad \blacksquare$

duo.speaker: Dr. Nova & Kaito
duo.title: Greenwood's Variance Formula & Confidence Envelopes

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Look at the denominator in Greenwood's formula: n-sub-i times n-sub-i minus d-sub-i! As tenure reaches sixty and seventy months, very few customers remain at risk, so n-sub-i shrinks and the confidence bands fan out dramatically!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Brilliant observation, Kaito. That widening trumpet shape warns analysts not to overfit long-term survival rates when only a handful of senior accounts remain at risk.

slides.title: Multicollinearity & Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) Dynamics

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova (Senior Architect)
solo.title: Multicollinearity & Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) Dynamics

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: In tabular enterprise systems, multicollinearity frequently arises from accounting definitions rather than natural physics. TotalCharges is approximately MonthlyCharges times tenure.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: When regressing TotalCharges against the other two, R-squared exceeds 0.98, pushing VIF beyond 50. This inflates standard errors by more than sevenfold and flips the sign of MonthlyCharges into negative, leading executives to false pricing conclusions.

solo.contentHtml:
Multicollinearity & The Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)

How deterministic billing identities produce catastrophic coefficient sign flips.

VIF Mathematical Definition
$$\text{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{1 - R_j^2}$$

$R_j^2$: coefficient of determination from regressing predictor $X_j$ against all other $p-1$ covariates.

Standard Error Inflation: $\text{SE}(\hat{\beta}_j) \propto \sqrt{\text{VIF}_j}$.
The Telco Billing Identity Pathology
$$\text{TotalCharges} \approx \text{MonthlyCharges} \times \text{tenure}$$
$R^2 > 0.98 \implies \text{VIF} > 50.0$!
  • • Sign Flip: $\hat{\beta}_{\text{MonthlyCharges}}$ flips from $+0.38$ (intuitive risk) to $-0.44$ (absurd claim that higher bills stop churn!).
  • • Resolution: Prune $\text{TotalCharges}$ or compute interaction term directly.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova

slides.title: The Geometry of High-Dimensional Space: Hypersphere Volume Collapse

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova
solo.title: The Geometry of High-Dimensional Space

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: In high dimensions, human spatial intuition developed in 2D and 3D fails completely. Consider an inscribed d-dimensional hypersphere of radius r placed inside a bounding hypercube of side length 2r.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: The volume of the hypercube is 2 to the d times r to the d. But by Gaussian polar integration, the hypersphere volume has a Gamma function in its denominator. Applying Stirling's approximation proves that the volume ratio collapses exponentially to zero as d increases!

solo.contentHtml:
The Geometry of High-Dimensional Space: Hypersphere Volume Collapse

Analytical proof that high-dimensional hypercubes concentrate virtually all volume in their outer corners.

Mathematical Formulation: Volume Ratio Proof

Consider inscribed hypersphere $S_d(r)$ inside hypercube $C_d(2r)$. The respective volumes are:

$$\text{Vol}(C_d(2r)) = (2r)^d = 2^d r^d, \quad \text{Vol}(S_d(r)) = \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2} + 1\right)} r^d$$

Taking the ratio $\rho(d) = \frac{\text{Vol}(S_d)}{\text{Vol}(C_d)}$ and applying Stirling's approximation $\Gamma(z+1) \sim \sqrt{2\pi z}(z/e)^z$:

$$\rho(d) \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi d}} \left( \frac{\pi e}{2d} \right)^{d/2} \xrightarrow{d \to \infty} \mathbf{0}$$
Empirical Numerical Ratio Reality
Dimension ($d$) Volume Ratio $\rho(d)$ Physical Interpretation
2$\pi / 4 \approx 78.54\%$Circle fills most of square
3$\pi / 6 \approx 52.36\%$Sphere occupies over half of cube
10$\approx 0.249\%$Sphere holds under $1/400$th volume
20$\approx 2.46 \times 10^{-8}$Zero-density center ($0.000002\%$)
50$\approx 1.53 \times 10^{-28}$Completely vacant center core
The Empty Center Invariant: High-dimensional datasets uniformly sampled in hypercubes reside entirely in the spike-like corners. The hypersphere inscribed at the center is mathematically empty!

duo.speaker: Dr. Nova & Kaito
duo.title: The Geometry of High-Dimensional Space

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Look at the volume ratio formula, Kaito. At dimension 2, an inscribed circle takes up seventy-eight point five percent of the square. At dimension 3, a sphere takes fifty-two percent of the cube.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: What happens when we move to twenty or fifty dimensions, Doctor Nova? Does the sphere keep holding twenty or thirty percent?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Not even close! At dimension 20, the sphere holds less than one in forty million parts of the volume. By dimension 50, it collapses to ten to the negative twenty-eighth. The center of high-dimensional space is practically a vacuum!

slides.title: Concentration of Pairwise Distances & Metric Degradation

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova
solo.title: Concentration of Pairwise Distances

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: The second consequence of high dimensionality is the concentration of Euclidean distances. By the Weak Law of Large Numbers, the average squared coordinate distance converges to its population mean.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Fluctuations around this mean scale only as the square root of d. As a result, the relative contrast between the nearest neighbor and the farthest neighbor converges to zero. In R-100, all points become virtually equidistant!

solo.contentHtml:
Concentration of Pairwise Distances & Metric Degradation

Why standard Euclidean clustering and nearest-neighbor queries collapse in high-dimensional feature spaces.

Mathematical Formulation: Distance Contrast Limit

Let $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ have i.i.d. coordinates with finite variance $\sigma^2$. The squared Euclidean distance satisfies:

$$\frac{1}{d} D^2(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}) = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{j=1}^d (X_j - Y_j)^2 \xrightarrow{p} \mu_D$$

By the Central Limit Theorem, total distance scales with standard deviation $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{d})$ relative to mean $\mathcal{O}(d)$:

$$\lim_{d \to \infty} \frac{\text{dist}_{\max} - \text{dist}_{\min}}{\text{dist}_{\min}} = \mathbf{0}, \quad \text{CV} = \frac{\sigma_D}{\mu_D} \to 0$$
Operational Failures in Machine Learning
1. K-Means Partition Degeneracy: Because every point is roughly equidistant from cluster centroids, assignment probabilities approach uniform randomness $1/K$.
2. k-NN Classification Inversion: The 1-nearest neighbor and 100th-nearest neighbor differ in distance by less than $2\%$, allowing minor sensor noise to shuffle neighbors arbitrarily.
The Solution: Exploratory analysis must discover lower-dimensional manifolds or topological graph invariants rather than relying on raw high-dimensional Euclidean space.

duo.speaker: Dr. Nova & Kaito
duo.title: Concentration of Pairwise Distances

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Doctor Nova, if all points become equidistant in high dimensions, what does that mean for algorithms like K-Means or k-Nearest Neighbors?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: It renders them mathematically degenerate! If the distance to your closest neighbor is ten point zero and the distance to your farthest neighbor is ten point two, any tiny random fluctuation completely shuffles your nearest neighbors.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: So high-dimensional clustering on raw features is essentially assigning data points at random! That is why we need topological invariants that don't depend on coordinate distances.

slides.title: Topological Data Analysis: Coordinate-Free Geometric Invariants

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova
solo.title: Topological Data Analysis

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: To escape the metric fragility of high-dimensional Euclidean space, we turn to Topological Data Analysis, or TDA. Topology studies geometric properties that are invariant under stretching, bending, and continuous deformation.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Instead of forcing points into disconnected spherical clusters, topology extracts Betti numbers: beta zero for connected components, beta one for 1D circular loops, and beta two for hollow cavities. By the Euler-Poincaré theorem, the alternating sum yields the Euler characteristic chi.

solo.contentHtml:
Topological Data Analysis: Coordinate-Free Geometric Invariants

Characterizing continuous point cloud structure through algebraic topology and Betti invariants.

$\beta_0$: Connected Components

Counts distinct, disconnected sub-populations or clusters in the point cloud.

$\beta_0 = 1$ for a continuous connected ring or graph.
$\beta_1$: 1D Circular Loops

Identifies periodic cycles, cyclic attractors, and recurrent biological evolutionary pathways.

$\beta_1 = 1$ (Ring), $\beta_1 = 2$ (Figure-Eight).
$\chi$: Euler Characteristic

The fundamental topological index connecting combinatorial graphs to Betti invariants:

$$\chi = \sum_{k=0}^d (-1)^k \beta_k = V - E$$
The Euler Characteristic of a Ring Invariant

For a 1-dimensional closed topological ring with $\beta_0 = 1$ component and $\beta_1 = 1$ cycle: $$\chi = \beta_0 - \beta_1 = 1 - 1 = \mathbf{0} \iff V = E$$ Any discretized simplicial graph representing a single loop has exactly as many vertices as edges ($V=E$), proving structural fidelity without reference to coordinate scales!

duo.speaker: Dr. Nova & Kaito
duo.title: Topological Data Analysis

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Topology doesn't care if a circle is drawn large or small, stretched into an ellipse, or rotated in twenty dimensions. As long as the hole is preserved, its first Betti number beta one equals one.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: So if we have cell cycle trajectories, viral recombination events, or periodic financial cycles, topology sees the loop directly, while K-Means would just chop it into three arbitrary balls!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Exactly, Kaito! And by the Euler-Poincaré theorem, the number of vertices minus the number of edges in our reconstructed nerve graph equals exactly zero for any single loop.

slides.title: The Mapper Algorithm: Mathematical Formulation & Nerve Complex

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova
solo.title: The Mapper Algorithm

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: How do we construct topological graphs from finite tabular point clouds? We deploy Gunnar Carlsson's famous Mapper algorithm.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: First, we choose a continuous filter lens, like density or distance. Second, we create an overlapping open cover of the filter space. Third, we cluster pre-images within each interval using DBSCAN. Finally, we build the Nerve graph, drawing edges wherever clusters share common points!

solo.contentHtml:
The Mapper Algorithm: Mathematical Formulation & Nerve Complex

Step-by-step construction of coordinate-free simplicial nerve complexes from point clouds.

STAGE 1
Continuous Filter Lens

Choose scalar function $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ (e.g. $L_2$ distance from centroid, PCA1 score, or kernel density).

STAGE 2
Overlapping Cover

Partition $[f_{\min}, f_{\max}]$ into $N$ intervals $\mathcal{U} = \{U_1, \dots, U_N\}$ with overlap fraction $\delta \in (0, 1)$.

STAGE 3
Pullback Clustering

Apply DBSCAN($\epsilon$) on each pre-image $f^{-1}(U_k)$ to form disjoint sub-clusters: $f^{-1}(U_k) = \bigcup_j C_{k,j}$.

STAGE 4
The Nerve Complex

Vertices are clusters $v_{k,j}$. Edge $(v, w) \in E$ if and only if clusters share points: $C_{k,j} \cap C_{l,m} \neq \emptyset$.

The Borsuk Nerve Theorem Guarantee

If each cluster intersection is contractible (carries no higher-dimensional holes), the abstract Nerve complex $\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{C})$ is homotopy equivalent to the underlying geometric manifold. The graph preserves every branching flare and closed circular cycle!

duo.speaker: Dr. Nova & Kaito
duo.title: The Mapper Algorithm

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Doctor Nova, why is the overlap parameter delta so critical in Stage 2? What happens if delta is zero percent?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: If delta is zero, adjacent intervals never share points! Their intersection is empty, meaning zero edges are drawn in Stage 4, and the Nerve complex shatters into isolated, disconnected dots.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: And if delta is too large, say eighty percent, points in distant intervals overlap, creating false cross-cutting edges that collapse the hole! That is why we tune overlap in our upcoming lab.

slides.title: Massive-Scale GPU Visualization: Datashader Architecture

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova
solo.title: Massive-Scale GPU Visualization

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: When exploratory datasets scale to hundreds of millions of records—such as global taxi traces or aerial LiDAR surveys—standard vector rendering in the browser crashes from memory exhaustion.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Datashader re-architects visualization into an array aggregation pipeline. Rather than creating hundred million DOM nodes, it executes atomic pixel binning directly in GPU VRAM, followed by logarithmic dynamic-range equalization in under 150 milliseconds!

solo.contentHtml:
Massive-Scale GPU Visualization: Datashader Architecture

Decoupling rendering performance from dataset cardinality via in-VRAM atomic aggregation.

1. In-VRAM Atomic Binning ($A_{u,v}$)

For canvas of resolution $W \times H$, map each point $(x_i, y_i) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ into a discrete bin using parallel GPU atomic additions:

$$A_{u, v} = \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{I}\left( \lfloor W \cdot \tilde{x}_i \rfloor = u \;\land\; \lfloor H \cdot \tilde{y}_i \rfloor = v \right)$$

Because aggregation complexity is $\mathcal{O}(N)$ on massively parallel GPU CUDA cores, $100\text{M}$ points aggregate in under $80\text{ ms}$.

2. Logarithmic Equalization ($C_{u,v}$)

Linear colormaps saturate when bin counts span 5 orders of magnitude ($1$ to $100{,}000$ points per pixel). Datashader applies log equalization:

$$C_{u, v} = \frac{\log(1 + A_{u, v})}{\log(1 + \max_{j, k} A_{j, k})} \in [0.0, 1.0]$$

Reveals subtle density ripples in rural highways while preventing metropolitan cores from blinding the display.

Latency Benchmark ($N=100{,}000{,}000$ points): Datashader GPU: 142 ms • Matplotlib SVG: OOM Crash (>32 GB)

slides.title: Causal Discovery: Breaking Free from Observational Correlation

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova
solo.title: Causal Discovery Foundations

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: The greatest epistemological limit of standard EDA is that statistical correlation cannot establish causal direction. Does X cause Y, does Y cause X, or does a hidden confounder Z cause both?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Causal Discovery formalizes this challenge. Under the Causal Markov Condition, the joint probability distribution factorizes across the parents of each node. And under Faithfulness, statistical independencies directly mirror the topological structure of the graph.

solo.contentHtml:
Causal Discovery: Breaking Free from Observational Correlation

Inferring Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) from purely observational tabular data.

1. The Causal Markov Condition

Every variable $X_j$ in the DAG $\mathcal{G}$ is conditionally independent of its non-descendants given its direct causal parents $\text{Pa}(X_j)$:

$$P(X_1, \dots, X_p) = \prod_{j=1}^p P(X_j \mid \text{Pa}(X_j))$$

Enables factorizing complex joint distributions into localized modular causal mechanisms.

2. The Faithfulness Assumption

All conditional independencies observed in the distribution $P$ are structural consequences of the graph topology $\mathcal{G}$:

$$X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid S \iff X \text{ and } Y \text{ are } d\text{-separated by } S \text{ in } \mathcal{G}$$

Rules out pathological algebraic cancellations (e.g., two opposing causal paths exactly canceling to produce accidental zero correlation).

The Three Foundational Junctions: Chain: $X \to Z \to Y$ • Fork: $X \leftarrow Z \to Y$ • Collider: $X \to Z \leftarrow Y$

duo.speaker: Dr. Nova & Kaito
duo.title: Causal Discovery Foundations

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Kaito, if variable X and variable Y are correlated in an EDA scatter plot, can we tell if X causes Y?

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: No, because a common parent Z could cause both of them! A fork X left-arrow Z right-arrow Y creates statistical correlation even when X has zero causal influence on Y.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Exactly. But notice: if we condition on Z in a fork, X and Y become conditionally independent. Whereas in a collider where X and Y both point into Z, they start independent and become dependent when you condition on Z! That asymmetry is how we orient causal edges.

slides.title: The PC Algorithm: Skeletal Discovery & Conditional Independence

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova
solo.title: The PC Algorithm

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: The Peter-Clark, or PC algorithm, is the foundational constraint-based method for causal structure discovery. It begins with a complete, fully connected undirected graph.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: It systematically tests conditional independence using Fisher's Z-transform on partial correlation. As conditioning order k increases from zero to one to two, edges are removed whenever conditional independence is detected, storing the separating set.

solo.contentHtml:
The PC Algorithm: Skeletal Discovery & Conditional Independence

Systematic edge elimination via Fisher's Z-transformation of partial correlation.

Phase 1: Skeletal Edge Elimination
  1. Start with complete undirected graph $K_p$ connecting all variables.
  2. Set conditioning subset size $k = 0$ (unconditional independence).
  3. For each adjacent pair $(X, Y)$, test $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid S$ for all subsets $S \subseteq \text{Adj}(X) \setminus \{Y\}$ with $|S| = k$.
  4. If independent ($p > \alpha$), delete edge $X - Y$ and record $S$ as separating set $\text{Sepset}(X, Y)$.
  5. Increment $k \leftarrow k + 1$ until no vertex has degree $\ge k+1$.
Statistical Test: Fisher's $Z$-Transformation

For continuous Gaussian variables, test partial correlation $r_{XY \cdot S}$ using Fisher's transformation:

$$z(r_{XY \cdot S}) = \frac{1}{2} \ln\left( \frac{1 + r_{XY \cdot S}}{1 - r_{XY \cdot S}} \right)$$

Under $H_0: X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid S$, the normalized test statistic is asymptotically standard normal:

$$T = \sqrt{n - |S| - 3} \cdot z(r_{XY \cdot S}) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$$
✓ Guaranteed Correctness: Under faithfulness and infinite sample size, the PC skeleton recovers the true moral graph in polynomial time!

slides.title: Collider Orientation & Meek's Propagation Rules

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova
solo.title: Collider Orientation & Meek's Rules

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Once the undirected skeleton is complete, Phase 2 orients unshielded colliders, or v-structures. For every triple X connected to Z and Z connected to Y where X and Y are not connected, we inspect the separating set.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: If and only if the central node Z is NOT in the separating set of X and Y, we orient both arrows inward as X points to Z and Y points to Z! Then Meek's four logical rules propagate remaining directions without creating cycles or new colliders.

solo.contentHtml:
Collider Orientation & Meek's Propagation Rules

Transforming undirected skeletons into Completed Partially Directed Acyclic Graphs (CPDAGs).

Phase 2: Unshielded Collider Rule

For every unshielded triple $X - Z - Y$ where $X$ and $Y$ are non-adjacent:

$$\text{Orient } X \to Z \leftarrow Y \iff Z \notin \text{Sepset}(X, Y)$$

If $Z$ were in $\text{Sepset}(X, Y)$, conditioning on $Z$ would block the path (making it a chain or fork). Because $Z \notin \text{Sepset}(X, Y)$, $Z$ is a collider!

Phase 3: Meek's Propagation Rules
  • R1 (No New Colliders): If $X \to Y - Z$ and $X \not\sim Z$, orient $Y \to Z$. (Orienting $Y \leftarrow Z$ would create a false collider at $Y$).
  • R2 (Acyclic Invariant): If $X \to Y \to Z$ and $X - Z$, orient $X \to Z$. (Orienting $X \leftarrow Z$ would create a directed cycle).
  • R3 (Double Triangle): If $X - Y_1 \to Z$ and $X - Y_2 \to Z$ with $Y_1 \not\sim Y_2$, orient $X \to Z$.
Output: A CPDAG representing the Markov Equivalence Class. Reversible edges represent observational equivalence; directed edges represent invariant causal laws!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Aha! So the empty set separated them! Since Z wasn't needed to separate them, Z is not in the separating set. If Z had been needed, Z would be a mediating chain or common cause!

solo.title: Production Implementation

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: How do enterprise data platforms integrate advanced exploratory analytics into production? We build robust pipelines using scikit-tda, KeplerMapper, and causal-learn.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: In production TDA, we replace brute-force DBSCAN with spatial kd-trees to preserve O(N log N) scaling. In causal discovery, we run non-parametric bootstrap resampling across folds to quantify causal edge confidence intervals.

solo.contentHtml:
Production Implementation: Topological Mapper & Causal Discovery Pipelines

Architecture and scalability patterns for enterprise high-dimensional analytics.

1. Production TDA Mapper Pipeline (`kmapper`)
import kmapper as km
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

mapper = km.KeplerMapper(verbose=1)
lens = mapper.fit_transform(X, projection="l2norm")
graph = mapper.map(
    lens, X,
    cover=km.Cover(n_cubes=10, perc_overlap=0.35),
    clusterer=DBSCAN(eps=0.5, min_samples=5)
)
# Assert topological Betti invariants in CI/CD
assert len(graph["nodes"]) > 5
assert len(graph["links"]) >= len(graph["nodes"]) - 1

Automated tests evaluate whether branching flares and cycles remain stable across monthly retraining batches.

2. Production Causal Discovery (`causal-learn`)
from causallearn.search.ConstraintBased.PC import pc
from causallearn.utils.cit import fisherz

cg = pc(
    data=X_df.values,
    alpha=0.05,
    indep_test=fisherz,
    stable=True,
    uc_rule=0  # Meek orientation rules
)
# Extract learned CPDAG adjacency matrix
adj_matrix = cg.G.graph
# Assert critical intervention invariance

Prevents downstream deep learning models from learning spurious confounded shortcuts ($X \leftarrow Z \to Y$).
